d1:
A plume in the mantle while the Pacific plate slides over it, printing a chain of volcanoes that gets older to the north-west — the clearest ruler we have for plate motion.

With one caveat that this map has to state, because it draws the chain: hotspots are NOT fixed. Inter-hotspot motion is demonstrable before about 90 Ma, and the 47 Ma bend between the Hawaiian Ridge and the Emperor Seamounts is now widely interpreted as the plume moving south rather than as the Pacific plate changing direction. Any track drawn before ~90 Ma is a model output, not a measurement.
The only place a mid-ocean ridge rises above sea level, held up by a plume beneath the spreading Atlantic.

The North American plate riding south-west over a plume, leaving a track of calderas across the Snake River Plain. It is the ONLY hotspot on Earth consistently imaged from the deep mantle to the surface, which is the calibration for how confident any other plume card here should sound.
A plume beneath the equatorial Pacific whose islands are young enough that their species are still visibly diverging.
The plume that erupted the Deccan Traps, still burning under the Indian Ocean 66 million years later.
Three rifts meet over a plume here; two are opening the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, the third is splitting Africa itself.
The plume that erupted the Parana-Etendeka basalts and then wrote its track across the seafloor as the Walvis Ridge while the South Atlantic opened.
A plume that built one of the largest oceanic plateaus on Earth, and briefly gave the southern Indian Ocean a drowned micro-continent with forests on it.
A long Pacific seamount chain, the southern counterpart to Hawaii's track.
A South Atlantic plume with a distinctive deep-mantle chemical signature.
A Pacific plume whose islands rise steeply from deep water with almost no reef fringe.
A plume close to the East Pacific Rise; the interaction between the two builds an unusually broad volcanic ridge.
A plume sitting on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, thickening the crust and lifting the islands above the sea.
A slow-moving plume off north-west Africa; because the African plate barely moves over it, the islands stay volcanically active far longer than Hawaii's.
A plume beneath one of the largest swells on the ocean floor, raising the seabed more than two kilometres.
A chain of volcanoes running from the Atlantic onto the African continent — unusually, it crosses the ocean-continent boundary without a break.
Volcanism in the central Sahara that built mountains rising from the desert to over three kilometres.
The southernmost active volcano on Earth, holding a permanent lake of molten lava through the Antarctic winter.
A plume near a triple junction in the South Atlantic, and the most remote island on the planet.
A southern Indian Ocean plume; iron shed from its islands fertilises one of the largest plankton blooms in the world.

vw: Still visible, but draw it as a LAVA PLAIN, not a highland. The crust sagged into the space vacated as the lava rose, so the Columbia 'Plateau' is really a slightly depressed basin; the topographic highs are the Yakima folds, not the basalt surface itself.
d1: The youngest continental flood basalt province, laid down across the Pacific Northwest as the Yellowstone plume arrived beneath the continent.

vw: The Ethiopian Highlands ARE the flood basalt pile - the surface is almost entirely above 1,500 m and culminates at Ras Dashen, 4,550 m. The Main Ethiopian Rift now bisects it.
d1: Flood basalts over the Afar plume that domed up East Africa and began tearing it open — the rifting still going on today.

vw: The most intact silicic LIP landform on Earth: 1,500 x 240 km broadly above 1,800 m, reaching ~3,340 m, with the Barranca del Cobre cut deeper into it than the Grand Canyon. Welded ignimbrite is at least as durable as basalt.
d1: The largest silicic volcanic province on Earth: ignimbrite sheets across northern Mexico, erupted as the subducting Farallon slab rolled back and the crust above it began to tear open into the Gulf of California.

vw: Revised to 0 - the remnants ARE landforms, even though the Thulean plateau as a whole was split and drowned by the rift it caused. East Greenland preserves up to 2.5 km of basalt over 65,000 km2, the Faroes a ~6 km succession reaching 882 m, and Antrim ~3,086 km2. Iceland is new crust, not preserved 62 Ma plateau.
d1: Eruptions as Greenland and Europe parted. Carbon released here is a leading suspect for the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, the sharpest warming of the Cenozoic.

vw: About 500,000 km2 of the original ~1.5 million km² survives - roughly a third - still over 2 km thick, and its western edge IS the Western Ghats escarpment: 900-1,500 m of relief running ~1,600 km, rising to Anamudi at 2,695 m.
d1: Vast basalt flows across western India, erupting as the subcontinent drove north over the Reunion plume. Their peak brackets the Chicxulub impact, and the two together ended the Cretaceous.

vw: Survives as coastal strips (Androy, Mailaka, Analalava). Crucially, Madagascar's central highlands are Precambrian basement, NOT the 88 Ma basalts - so this province is not the island's defining relief and should not be drawn as such. LOW CONFIDENCE.
d1: Eruptions as Madagascar separated from India, leaving the island isolated — and its life to evolve alone.

vw: The oceanic plateau that stops being a plateau. Its crust is 10-20 km thick, straddling the ~17 km threshold below which plateaus subduct normally, so its margins were obducted onto Colombia, Ecuador, Costa Rica and Curacao while the interior was trapped in an enclosed basin and smoothed flat by terrigenous fill. Still thickened crust; no longer bathymetric relief. LOW CONFIDENCE on the date.
d1: Built by the Galapagos plume on the floor of the Pacific and then rammed into the gap between the Americas, where it survives as the thick, buoyant crust under the Caribbean Sea — one of the few oceanic plateaus that escaped subduction by being too light to sink. Its eruption is the leading trigger for OCEANIC ANOXIC EVENT 2 (Bonarelli, ~94.3-93.5 Ma), when the deep ocean ran out of oxygen at the hottest moment of the last 200 million years. See the climate-events panel.

vw: Still the largest and thickest oceanic plateau on Earth: 1.5-1.86 million km², crust 33 km, crest ~1,700 m against a 4,500-5,000 m abyssal floor. Draw it WHOLE - over 90 percent is intact. It did not subduct; it jammed the Vitiaz trench and forced a subduction polarity reversal, with only the SW margin deforming and slices obducted onto Malaita and Santa Isabel.
d1: The largest oceanic plateau on Earth: 1.86 million square kilometres of sea floor, erupted in a few million years. It is the leading trigger for OCEANIC ANOXIC EVENT 1a (Selli, ~120.5-119.3 Ma) — the carbon-isotope record swings hard at exactly its eruption, and calcareous nannoplankton went through a sharp crisis. See the climate-events panel.

vw: 770,000 km2 with a crest at 2,500-3,000 m and crust 21-25 km thick; rifted from Ontong Java Nui.
d1: One of three fragments of Ontong Java Nui, a single Cretaceous mega-plateau that a spreading triple junction later split apart.

vw: Still a plateau but the most damaged of the three: ~400,000 km2 survives of an original ~800,000. It jammed the Chatham Rise at ~100 Ma and is now partly subducting beneath the North Island, imaged 37-140 km down.
d1: The third fragment of Ontong Java Nui. Too buoyant to sink easily, it is now jamming into the subduction zone beneath New Zealand.

vw: The Alpha Ridge carries 38 km of crust - thicker than Ontong Java - with 2,700 m of relief and a crest at ~1,250 m. Worth splitting in the renderer: Alpha and Mendeleev ridges submarine, Svalbard, Franz Josef Land and Ellesmere subaerial.
d1: Magmatism spanning the Arctic as the Amerasia Basin opened, from Svalbard to the Sverdrup Basin and the Alpha Ridge.

vw: After CAMP, the best example of a giant province that is not a landform. Its main surviving record is reworked volcanic detritus in the Eromanga and Great Artesian basins; Coral Sea rifting at ~62-52 Ma removed most of the rest.
d1: A vast silicic province along eastern Australia. Unusually for a province this size it is driven by slab rollback rather than a mantle plume.

vw: Only ~4,100 km2 is exposed against ~200,000 km2 buried under the Bengal Basin - about 2 percent visible. Killed by burial, not erosion: the rock is fine, the landform is gone.
d1: The Kerguelen plume's first arrival under eastern India, before the plate carried the continent onward.

vw: The Brazilian Serra Geral remains a major plateau and escarpment; Etendeka is a much smaller severed remnant. Split by South Atlantic opening, with the Walvis Ridge and Rio Grande Rise marking the join.
d1: One province split in two: its halves now sit in Brazil and Namibia, torn apart by the opening South Atlantic.
A large igneous province: flood basalts erupted over a geologically brief interval, on a scale with no modern equivalent.

vw: Ignimbrite plateaus of the Deseado Massif and the Antarctic Peninsula still stand with moderate relief after 150 Myr, though much is buried under the Austral-Magallanes and San Jorge basins. LOW CONFIDENCE - not verified against a primary source.
d1: One of the largest silicic provinces known, erupted across Patagonia and the Antarctic Peninsula as the Weddell Sea began to open.

vw: Ceased to be a plateau when it accreted, but survives in a way no other province does: it kept its full 25-30 km crustal thickness (usually accretion strips plateaus to 8-15 km) and is now the Wrangell-St Elias Mountains, Vancouver Island and Haida Gwaii. Accretion age genuinely spans 160-100 Ma in the literature. Caveat: its exposed section includes subaerial flows, so it may never have been a classic deep-ocean plateau.
d1: An oceanic plateau erupted in Panthalassa and later rammed into North America, where it now forms a belt of accreted crust from Vancouver Island to Alaska. It is the leading suspect for the Carnian Pluvial Episode.

vw: The oldest surviving oceanic plateau, and empirical proof that isostatic relief outlasts thermal subsidence: Tamu Massif's summit is at ~1,980 m against a ~6,400 m base, giving ~4,460 m of relief after 145 Myr, on 26 km of crust.
d1: A huge Pacific plateau built at a three-way junction of spreading ridges. Whether a plume or the junction itself made it is still argued.

vw: The key negative result, and the largest province by area (~11 million km²) with almost no topographic legacy at all. It was never a plateau: Newark Basin flows are sandwiched between lacustrine formations, buried by rift-basin subsidence within ~100,000 years of eruption; the Amazonian sills were emplaced at depth; the Moroccan basalts survive precisely BECAUSE they were buried. The Palisades cliffs are an intrusion exhumed in the Pleistocene, not a preserved lava surface. Show CAMP erupting and then vanishing almost at once - that is what actually happened.
d1: Magmatism spread across four continents as Pangaea began to split, opening the crack that became the Atlantic. It coincides with the end-Triassic extinction.

vw: The Putorana Plateau is the surviving high ground, 800 x 500 km with Mount Kamen at 1,678 m and the classic trap step-topography intact after 252 Myr on cold, dead craton - the longest-surviving flood basalt landform of the Phanerozoic bar Kalkarindji.
d1: The largest continental flood basalt known: perhaps four million cubic kilometres of lava across Siberia in under a million years, and — as it burned through coal and evaporite — enough carbon and sulphur to acidify the oceans and drive the end-Permian extinction, the worst in Earth's history.

vw: Over 250,000 km2 survives - about half - up to 5.5 km thick. But note the modern Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau elevation is Cenozoic and Tibet-related: the basalt is resistant caprock on a young plateau, re-exhumed, not a continuously surviving Permian landform.
d1: Flood basalts in South China, associated with the end-Guadalupian extinction some eight million years before the far larger end-Permian crisis.

vw: Only 105 km2 of lava flows are exposed today. Pillow lavas and hyaloclastites show partly submarine emplacement, followed by progressive thermo-tectonic subsidence of the Indian passive margin. The modern Pir Panjal elevation is Neogene Himalayan tectonics re-using old rock, NOT a surviving Permian landform - correcting an easy misreading.
d1: Flood basalts in Kashmir that rifted the Cimmerian terranes off Gondwana and opened the Neotethys Ocean behind them.

vw: Largely buried under Tarim Basin sediment, cropping out only at the Keping and Bachu uplifts. LOW CONFIDENCE.
d1: Early Permian magmatism beneath what is now the Tarim Basin, erupted through the heart of central Asia.

vw: Preserved as dyke swarms and sills around the Oslo Rift and Skagerrak; the volcanic edifice did not survive Permian-Triassic rifting and burial.
d1: Late Carboniferous magmatism across northern Europe as Pangaea finished assembling and the crust behind the collision began to pull apart.

vw: Mostly buried under the Dnieper-Donets and Pripyat basin fills; the Kola alkaline complexes survive as intrusive roots only.
d1: Late Devonian rift volcanism across the East European craton, close in age to the Frasnian-Famennian extinction.

vw: Dismembered and buried by the accretionary tectonics of the Central Asian Orogenic Belt.
d1: Devonian plume volcanism in central Asia, erupted through the collage of arcs and terranes that would become Siberia's southern margin.

vw: A small sill-and-volcanic province caught up in the Verkhoyansk fold belt; no primary landform survives.
d1: Ordovician magmatism on the Siberian platform, roughly contemporary with the great diversification of marine life.

vw: A sill province on the Siberian craton margin; ~975 Myr of burial and Verkhoyansk deformation leave no topographic trace.
d1: Magmatism on the eastern Siberian craton around a billion years ago, at the far edge of this reconstruction.

vw: Dominantly the Vilyui and Chara-Sinsk dyke swarms plus basalts buried under the Vilyui Basin. LOW CONFIDENCE.
d1: Late Devonian flood basalts that tore open the eastern Siberian platform, and the leading candidate for the Frasnian-Famennian extinction that removed most reef-building life.

vw: If confirmed, the record-holder for flood-basalt landform longevity at ~511 Myr: the Antrim Plateau Volcanics sit on arid, stable Australian craton, the single most favourable preservation setting there is. MEDIUM CONFIDENCE - verify against a primary source before shipping, since a 511 Myr surviving landform is a strong claim.
d1: Australia's Cambrian flood basalts, linked to an early-Cambrian extinction pulse not long after animals first diversified.

vw: Rift volcanics along the Iapetan margins were buried by the passive margin sequence, then caught in the Appalachian-Caledonian orogenies.
d1: Rift volcanism as Rodinia's fragments finally separated and the Iapetus Ocean opened between them.

vw: Draw as a DYKE PROVINCE, not a plateau. The Franklin dyke swarm, Coronation sills and Natkusiak basalts survive, and the sills form ramparts and linear sets of islands - but that is Phanerozoic differential erosion picking out resistant intrusions, not a surviving 719 Ma landform. Its climatic importance is front-loaded anyway: the CO2 drawdown came from weathering FRESH tropical basalt within ~2 Myr of eruption.
d1: Enormous eruptions across what is now Arctic Canada at the threshold of the Sturtian glaciation. Weathering of fresh basalt in the tropics is thought to have drawn down enough CO2 to help freeze the planet.

vw: A dyke swarm; whatever volcanic cover existed was removed before the Cambrian.
d1: Rift magmatism along the edge of Laurentia as Rodinia began to come apart, well before the supercontinent finally broke.

vw: Dyke swarms and thin volcanics within the Adelaide Rift Complex; no surviving relief.
d1: Early Neoproterozoic dyke swarms across Australia, marking the first tearing of Rodinia's interior.

vw: Volcanics and intrusions in the Jiangnan belt, buried beneath Cryogenian glacial and Sinian marine sequences.
d1: Plume magmatism beneath the South China block during Rodinia's breakup, in the run-up to the Cryogenian glaciations.

vw: Dyke swarms across the Sao Francisco and Congo cratons; the volcanic carapace is entirely gone.
d1: Dykes and sills across the joined Sao Francisco and Congo cratons, erupted as Rodinia stretched after assembling.

vw: A dyke swarm in the Pilbara with no preserved extrusive component; valuable as a paleomagnetic anchor, not as a landform.
d1: A dyke swarm across the Pilbara of Western Australia, and one of the anchor points for reconstructing where Australia sat within Rodinia.
The rift that is currently splitting Africa. Projected forward, it floods and becomes an ocean.
Projected volcanism where Africa drives into Europe and the Mediterranean closes, raising a mountain chain along the suture.
Projected arc volcanism along the closing ocean between the converging continents of the future supercontinent.

vw: A dyke swarm on the North China craton with no extrusive remnant.
d1: A dyke swarm across the North China craton, and the likely conjugate of the Bahia- Gangila dykes in South America and Africa — evidence for how those blocks were joined a billion years ago.

vw: Bimodal volcanics on the Yangtze craton, buried by the Nanhua rift fill.
d1: Bimodal volcanism on the Yangtze craton, part of the long sequence of eruptions that accompanied Rodinia's breakup in South China.

vw: Mafic-ultramafic intrusions along the western Yangtze margin, buried beneath Sinian cover.
d1: One of a series of magmatic pulses beneath South China as Rodinia came apart, feeding the rift basins that later filled with glacial debris.

vw: Silicic volcanics and granites still crop out in Rajasthan, but as low desert inselbergs; the original ignimbrite plateau was stripped by the early Paleozoic.
d1: One of the largest silicic provinces of the Precambrian: rhyolites and granites across Rajasthan, erupted as Rodinia stretched. Its rocks record where India sat inside the supercontinent.

vw: Sills and volcanics on the southern Siberian craton margin, buried and then caught in Baikalide deformation.
d1: Magmatism on the southern edge of the Siberian craton, proposed as a continuation of the Franklin event and so as part of what tipped Earth into the Sturtian glaciation.

vw: A dyke swarm in the Gariep belt, deformed by Pan-African orogeny.
d1: A dyke swarm in southern Africa of the same age as the Franklin eruptions in Arctic Canada, on the other side of a world about to freeze over.

vw: Preserved but buried beneath the East European Platform cover.
d1: Ediacaran flood basalts across what is now Ukraine, erupted as Baltica pulled away from the rest of Rodinia — and close in time to the first large, soft-bodied animals.

vw: A deep-crustal intrusive complex exhumed only by Caledonian orogeny; it never had a preserved surface expression. Also allochthonous - it sits in the Kalak Nappe, so its present coordinates are not where it formed.
d1: A deep-crustal magmatic province in Arctic Norway, emplaced as the Iapetus Ocean began to open. What is exposed is its plumbing, not its volcanoes.

vw: Buried under the Anadarko Basin, then partly exhumed as the Wichita Mountains during the Pennsylvanian - a re-exposed root, not a surviving plateau.
d1: Cambrian rift volcanism and layered intrusions along a failed arm of the opening Iapetus. Buried for 300 million years, then shoved back into daylight as the Wichita Mountains when Pangaea assembled.

vw: Sills near the Lena mouth, incorporated into the Verkhoyansk belt.
d1: Cambrian sills near the mouth of the Lena, erupted at roughly the same time as Australia's Kalkarindji basalts on the far side of the world.

vw: Deformed into the Alborz range during Cimmerian and later collisions.
d1: Ordovician volcanism along the northern edge of Gondwana, and one of very few candidates in a stretch of time otherwise almost empty of large igneous provinces.

vw: Dolerite sills armour the Transantarctic Mountains the length of the range, preserved by polar-desert conditions for 183 Myr.
d1: The Antarctic half of the Karoo-Ferrar event: dolerite sheets injected the length of the Transantarctic Mountains, whose dark banded cliffs are this magma frozen in place.

vw: Carried into the Himalayan collision zone and deformed; no plateau survives, only tectonised basalt and dykes in southern Tibet.
d1: The Kerguelen plume's opening act on the Gondwanan side, now folded into southern Tibet — carried half the world from the province it was erupted with.

vw: A small but intact Late Jurassic Pacific plateau - among the oldest surviving seafloor topography anywhere.
d1: A small Late Jurassic plateau, and one of the oldest surviving pieces of seafloor topography anywhere on the planet.

vw: Largely buried under the Perth Basin's Cretaceous-Cenozoic fill.
d1: The Australian half of the Kerguelen plume's arrival, erupted just before the continent tore away and now buried beneath the Perth Basin.
The southern twin of the Tristan plume. The two built the Walvis Ridge together and then separated into distinct chemical lineages — evidence that a single plume can be striped.

vw: A broad guyot-capped rise; the flat tops record subsidence from sea level, so it was once an island chain and is now a drowned one.
d1: A broad Cretaceous rise whose volcanoes once broke the surface as islands with coral reefs; they have since subsided into flat-topped seamounts drowned a kilometre down.

One of the longest hotspot tracks on Earth, running from the Monteregian Hills of Quebec through the White Mountains and the New England Seamounts to a drowned volcano in the mid-Atlantic. North America slid clean over it.

vw: The main body of a 1.23 million km² edifice rising 2,000 m above the surrounding basins. Note it was LAND: ODP recovered fossil wood, charcoal- bearing soils and river-transported clasts, and at its peak this was an island of ~500,000 km2 with peaks 1,000-2,000 m above sea level. Final drowning ~20 Ma.
d1: The main body of a drowned volcanic continent a third the size of Australia. Cores drilled from it contain wood and coal — it had forests before it sank.
A South Pacific plume whose track can be followed back through the Cook-Austral chain into the Tuvalu, Gilbert and Marshall islands — possibly the oldest hotspot still erupting in the Pacific.

vw: Buried beneath the Bengal Basin's Himalayan sediment load; only the Shillong Plateau margin still exposes it.
d1: The eastern twin of the Rajmahal Traps, erupted in the same pulse over the Kerguelen plume and now buried under the sediment of the Bengal delta.

vw: Strongly asymmetric: crest at ~2,161 m in the south deepening to 4,637 m in the north. Vesicular non-pillowed trachyte flows show it was probably above sea level early in its history.
d1: A mid-Cretaceous plateau on the Pacific floor, built while the ocean was making new crust faster than at any time since. Its lavas erupted into air, not water — it stood above the sea before it sank.

vw: Still bathymetrically prominent, with Heard Island (Mont Ross, 1,850 m) and the Kerguelen archipelago emergent above it.
d1: The middle segment of the Kerguelen edifice, built as the plume continued to feed the growing plateau after India had moved on.

vw: 300,000 km2 standing 2.5 km above the surrounding seafloor with a summit at 2,500 m depth and crust 20-25 km thick.
d1: A basalt plateau south of Africa, erupted as the last threads between Africa and Antarctica parted. It still rises two and a half kilometres above the surrounding seafloor.

vw: The Antarctic third of the same 1.2 million km² plateau, whose relief still steers the Weddell Gyre and opens the recurring Weddell Polynya.
d1: The Antarctic counterpart of the Agulhas Plateau, split from it as the Southern Ocean opened. Its bulk still steers the currents above it, opening a recurring hole in the winter sea ice.

vw: A shallow bathymetric ridge in the eastern Indian Ocean, rifted off the Central Kerguelen Plateau in the Eocene; its flank stood ~2,000 m above sea level at the moment of rifting.
d1: The rifted-off northern edge of the Kerguelen Plateau, carried away when a spreading ridge cut the plateau in two during the Eocene.
The plume that split Madagascar from India and erupted the Madagascar flood basalts, leaving the island alone in the Indian Ocean with its own evolutionary experiment.
A plume beneath the South Atlantic that first surfaced inland, erupting diamond- bearing kimberlites across Brazil before the continent carried on west and left it offshore.
A chain of seamounts in the central Indian Ocean, and one of the harder features to reconcile with a fixed-plume model.
A slow plume off Iberia whose track runs north-east along the Tore Rise; like the Canaries, it stays active because Africa barely moves.
A plume that never built a chain but lifted a broad swell of seafloor. Bermuda itself is a single drowned volcano capped by limestone.

vw: The youngest and shallowest segment, carrying the Kerguelen Islands.
d1: The youngest segment, still fed by the plume and still carrying islands above water in the far southern Indian Ocean.
A South Atlantic plume near the ridge, one of a cluster whose chemistry samples the edge of the African deep-mantle pile.
The most active volcano in the Austral chain, a seamount that occasionally boils the sea surface without ever quite breaching it.
A north-east Pacific plume whose seamount chain runs into the Juan de Fuca Ridge, where plume and ridge have been interacting for tens of millions of years.
A hotspot Australia has been sliding over for thirty million years, leaving the longest continental volcanic track on Earth — a line of dead volcanoes from Queensland to Victoria.

vw: The conjugate half of the same 30 Ma plateau, severed by Red Sea and Gulf of Aden opening and now standing as the Yemen highlands.
d1: The other half of the Afar flood basalts, erupted at the same moment as the Ethiopian Traps and then torn away from them as the Red Sea opened. The two plateaus now face each other across the water.
A western Pacific plume whose track runs through the Caroline Islands and carries some of the ocean's deepest-rooted volcanic chemistry.
A plume off Chile whose islands are carried east toward the trench, where the ridge it built jams into the Andean subduction zone.
A plume beneath West Antarctica, feeding volcanoes that erupt through the ice sheet and melt it from below.
A small Atlantic plume off north-east Brazil, its islands the eroded necks of volcanoes that never grew large.
A plume in the Tasman Sea whose oldest island has eroded to a spire of rock rising six hundred metres straight out of the ocean.
A Pacific plume with an unusual twist: it sits beside the tearing corner of the Tonga trench, which pulls its magma sideways.
A Gulf of Alaska plume whose seamount chain bends north toward the Aleutian trench, mirroring the Hawaiian track on a smaller scale.
A hotspot that printed a line of seamounts down the Tasman Sea while the Australian plate raced north over it.
A southern Pacific plume whose seamount chain runs from near the East Pacific Rise toward the Tuamotus.
A plume between Africa and Madagascar; its newest volcano grew from the seafloor off Mayotte within the last decade, and was detected by the earthquakes it made on the way up.
A young Pacific plume whose islands are so isolated they were the last refuge of the Bounty mutineers.
A plume beneath French Polynesia, building the high volcanic islands that subside into the ring-shaped atolls Darwin explained.

slw: BURIED ALMOST IMMEDIATELY. A submarine crater on the Yucatan carbonate shelf, blanketed within a couple of million years and now under ~1 km of carbonate. It is traced only by a gravity anomaly and the ring of cenotes. Rendering it as a visible scar for 90 Myr is the layer's biggest persistence error — although its GLOBAL signature (see GLOBAL_EFFECT) is permanent, which is the opposite lesson.
ge: The only unambiguous impact-driven mass extinction in the record. A worldwide ejecta and iridium layer at 66.052 +/- 0.043 Ma, sulphate aerosol loading from the anhydrite-rich target, an impact winter lasting years, and the end of the non-avian dinosaurs. The topography vanished in ~2 Myr; the boundary clay is permanent and is found on every continent. If the app renders one thing that outlives its crater, it is this.
cfu: 66.038 +/- 0.098 Ma (Ar-Ar + U-Pb); boundary ejecta 66.052 +/- 0.043 Ma
d1: The asteroid that ended the Cretaceous. A ten-kilometre body struck the Yucatan shelf, throwing enough rock and sulphur into the atmosphere to darken and chill the planet for years, and taking the non-avian dinosaurs with it.

slw: STILL. An eroded but well-exposed tundra basin, now a UNESCO geopark.
ge: Source of the older late Eocene clinopyroxene-bearing spherule layer, geochemically tied to the crater (Whitehead et al. 2000, EPSL). A global stratigraphic marker. Note this is a DIFFERENT layer from the North American tektites — Popigai and Chesapeake Bay are separated by at least ~0.5 and possibly ~3 Myr, so the late Eocene 'cluster' is a sequence, not a pair.
cfu: 35.7 +/- 0.2 Ma (Bottomley et al. 1997); 36.63 +/- 0.92 Ma recalculated by S&K 2020
d1: A Siberian crater whose impact shocked graphite into diamond across the surrounding rock. It falls in a late Eocene cluster of strikes.

slw: STILL. The 'Eye of Quebec' — an annular reservoir ring around Ile Rene-Levasseur. 215 Myr old and the most recognisable crater on Earth from orbit. Proof that a large crater in stable Grenvillian basement can outlast the fade window by a factor of two.
ge: A candidate source for a Late Triassic (Rhaetian/Norian) distal spherule bed reported from the Bristol Channel, UK (Walkden et al. 2002). The correlation is reasonable but not as tight as the Chicxulub or Popigai cases, and Manicouagan is NOT a mass-extinction trigger — it predates the end-Triassic event by ~14 Myr.
cfu: 215.56 +/- 0.05 Ma (U-Pb zircon) — among the best-dated craters on Earth
d1: A Late Triassic crater, its ring-shaped lake now one of the most recognisable features from orbit.

slw: STILL, in outline. Deeply eroded into the Gawler Range Volcanics, but the circular playa of Lake Acraman is obvious from orbit after ~580 Myr.
ge: A distal ejecta horizon traced over 300 km into the Bunyeroo Formation of the Flinders Ranges. The layer is stratigraphically interleaved with early acritarch and Ediacaran biotic change, which is why the crater is dated from the ejecta rather than the other way round.
cfu: ~580 Ma; Impact Earth brackets 541-635 Ma. Age is INDIRECT — from the Bunyeroo Fm ejecta horizon, not the crater
d1: An Ediacaran impact in South Australia. Its ejecta layer sits in rocks alongside some of the earliest complex organisms.

slw: Completely buried beneath Kalahari sand. Found by its magnetic signature — literally invisible.
cfu: 146.06 +/- 0.16 Ma (U-Pb); sits on the Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary
d1: A Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary crater buried under the Kalahari, found only by its magnetic signature.

slw: Deeply eroded on Pay-Khoy and partly submerged under the Kara Sea. Carries impact diamonds.
cfu: 70.7 +/- 2.2 Ma (Ar-Ar, Trieloff et al. 1998, recalc. S&K 2020). Reject the uncited 75.34 +/- 0.66 Ma
d1: A confirmed impact structure roughly 65 km across, formed about 70.7 million years ago.

slw: TOPOGRAPHY ENTIRELY GONE. Tectonically dismembered by Cordilleran thrusting; there is no crater form left anywhere. It is known almost solely from a huge shatter-cone field smeared across thrust sheets, and even its centre is inferred — published positions disagree by over a degree.
cfu: 470-900 Ma bracket. Structure is tectonically dismembered; no direct date exists
d1: One of the oldest large craters in North America, its structure dismembered and scattered by later mountain building.

slw: Buried under ~900 m of Eromanga Basin sediment. Known from seismic plus 31 petroleum wells — there is no surface expression at all.
ge: A distal ejecta blanket across roughly 400,000 km2 of the Eromanga Basin, pinned to the Barremian/Aptian boundary. The ejecta is the only reason the age is known at all — the crater itself is undated. Impact into a shallow epicontinental sea, so there is a resurge and tsunami signature too.
cfu: 125 +/- 1 Ma, but a STRATIGRAPHIC tie to the Barremian/Aptian boundary, not a radiometric date. Impact Earth: 121.8-123.8 Ma
d1: An Early Cretaceous impact into a shallow Australian sea, now buried under the Eromanga Basin.

slw: Partially survives as the semicircular St Lawrence embayment, with Mont des Eboulements as the central uplift. Still a seismically active zone — the weakened rock localises modern earthquakes 450 Myr later.
cfu: 450 +/- 20 Ma (U-Pb shocked zircon, Schmieder et al. 2019); S&K bracket ~453-430 Ma
d1: An Ordovician crater on the St. Lawrence; the modern river follows the weakened rock around its rim. Long dated to the Carboniferous, it was reassigned to ~450 Ma by U-Pb on shocked zircon.

slw: STILL, partially. Sweden's ring of lakes traces the rim depression around the central uplift after 380 Myr — the crater floor was eroded away but the ring of softer downfaulted sediment survives as topography.
d1: A Devonian crater in Sweden, the largest in Europe, its ring of lakes still visible in the landscape.

slw: STILL. Lake Karakul at 3,900 m in the Pamirs fills most of the structure. High- altitude aridity has preserved it, whatever its true age.
cfu: NO radiometric age exists. Only '<60 Ma'. The 25 Ma in the list has no standing; legacy EID said '<5 Ma'
d1: A confirmed impact structure roughly 52 km across, formed about 25.0 million years ago.

slw: Submarine on the Scotian Shelf; buried beneath the seafloor and found only by petroleum drilling.
d1: A confirmed impact structure roughly 45 km across, formed about 51.1 million years ago.

slw: Buried ~200 m deep in Alberta and now a producing oil and gas field.
cfu: Three live candidates: ~91, ~132 +/- 1.3, ~141 Ma. S&K bracket ~383-108 Ma. Impact Earth: 108-383 Ma
d1: A confirmed impact structure roughly 25 km across, formed about 141.0 million years ago.

slw: Buried under 300-500 m of Coastal Plain sediment. But it never stopped MATTERING: it still steers the modern bay, drives a groundwater salinity anomaly and causes measurable land subsidence. A case where 'scar' and 'influence' diverge.
ge: Source of the North American tektite/microtektite strewn field, a global marker horizon. Separately and unusually, it still exerts a physical influence today: it controls the shape of the modern Chesapeake Bay, drives a deep groundwater salinity anomaly across the lower Delmarva Peninsula, and causes measurable ongoing land subsidence — 35 Myr after the fact.
cfu: 34.86 +/- 0.32 Ma (Ar-Ar on melt rock and tektites)
d1: A late Eocene strike on the North American shelf; the buried crater still steers the modern bay and its groundwater.

slw: STILL, in fact — a well-exposed granite central uplift with concentric ring valleys, obvious from orbit after 255 Myr. South America's largest.
ge: Falls within uncertainty of the Permian-Triassic boundary, and the association is much discussed. But at 40 km it is roughly two orders of magnitude too small in energy to drive the end-Permian extinction; the Siberian Traps are. The existing EVENT_NOTES entry already states this correctly and should be kept.
cfu: 254.7 +/- 2.5 Ma (Tohver et al. 2012, U-Pb + Ar-Ar). Supersedes 244.4 Ma. Impact Earth brackets 248-264 Ma
d1: Brazil's largest crater, its age falling within uncertainty of the end-Permian extinction, though it is far too small to be its cause.

slw: On the floor of the Barents Sea, entirely submarine and now buried. Known only from seismic and drilling.
ge: Impact into the shallow Jurassic-Cretaceous Barents seaway generated a documented resurge and tsunami signature in the surrounding basin, and an iridium anomaly is reported in the Volgian nearby. A claimed correlative tsunami deposit in Sweden is speculative. Regional, not global — the existing EVENT_NOTES wording ('triggered a tsunami across the shallow Jurassic seaway') is appropriately scoped.
cfu: 142 +/- 2.6 Ma; Impact Earth brackets 141-145 Ma
d1: A crater on the floor of the Barents Sea, which triggered a tsunami across the shallow Jurassic seaway.

slw: Not exposed; buried under the Carnarvon Basin and known only from drilling into the central uplift.
cfu: NO reliable age. 364 +/- 8 Ma is K-Ar on authigenic clay, formally disputed. S&K/Impact Earth: 168-2005 Ma bracket
d1: A crater buried under the Carnarvon Basin east of Shark Bay, known only from drilling into its central uplift. Its age is genuinely unknown — the only radiometric date is on authigenic clay and was formally disputed — so the stratigraphy permits anything from the Devonian to the Proterozoic.

slw: Buried under Jurassic red beds and glacial till, though Lake St Martin's outline partly reflects it.
d1: A confirmed impact structure roughly 40 km across, formed about 227.8 million years ago.

slw: Buried under Neogene and Quaternary cover; impactites crop out only in Volga bank cuts.
cfu: 195.9 +/- 1.0 Ma (Holm-Alwmark et al. 2019)
d1: A large Early Jurassic structure on the Russian platform, now almost entirely buried.

slw: Survives as an exposed ring of Carswell Formation dolomite. Notable for a practical reason: impact-remobilised uranium ore hosts the Cluff Lake mine.
cfu: 481.5 +/- 0.8 Ma (Ar-Ar adularia). Caveat: dates hydrothermal circulation, a close minimum
d1: A confirmed impact structure roughly 39 km across, formed about 481.5 million years ago.

slw: STILL. A lake with a central ring of melt-rock islands. Glacial scour sharpened rather than erased it.
cfu: 286.2 +/- 2.6 Ma (Ar-Ar plateau)
d1: The larger of the two Clearwater lakes. The pair look like a classic double impact, but their ages differ by nearly 200 million years — they are unrelated.

slw: The largest fully-onshore US structure and completely buried under glacial drift; known only from drillcore.
cfu: 75.9 +/- 0.1 Ma (Ar-Ar) — one of the tightest in the catalogue
d1: An Iowa crater once proposed as the killer of the dinosaurs, until redating placed it about ten million years too early.

slw: Deeply eroded in remote Arnhem Land; a prominent central uplift with a >=20 km collar of upturned and overturned beds is all that remains.
d1: A confirmed impact structure roughly 25 km across, formed about 657 million years ago.

slw: A special case: superbly preserved BENEATH ~930 m of the Greenland Ice Sheet. It was a surface feature in a rainforest landscape for tens of Myr, then sealed by ice rather than eroded. The only known subglacial crater.
cfu: 57.99 +/- 0.54 Ma (Ar-Ar + U-Pb, Kenny et al. 2022)
d1: Buried under a kilometre of the Greenland ice sheet and found by radar. It is far older than the ice: when it formed, the target was rainforest.

slw: Only the central uplift survives, emerging as an archipelago in Lake Superior. The rest is drowned and eroded. The islands' rocks are full of shatter cones.
cfu: ~450 Ma, poorly constrained, no formal uncertainty published
d1: An archipelago in Lake Superior that is the central uplift of an Ordovician crater, its rocks full of shatter cones.

slw: STILL. Lake Kamestastin with a central-uplift island; the prime terrestrial analogue site for lunar impact melt.
d1: A confirmed impact structure roughly 28 km across, formed about 37.91 million years ago.

slw: STILL. Lake-filled after 465 Myr — remarkable persistence, again thanks to glacial excavation of the weakened rock.
cfu: 460-470 Ma apparent ages. 465 is a computed midpoint, NOT a published value
d1: The smaller Clearwater lake, and the older by far. Its Ordovician age is what disproved the twin-impact story its shape suggests.

slw: Deeply eroded on Victoria Island with no topographic rim; recognised in 2010 only from shatter-coned bedrock and ring-disturbed strata visible from the air.
cfu: 430-450 Ma bracket (Ar-Ar)
d1: An Arctic crater recognised only in 2010, its rim visible from the air as a ring of disturbed strata.

slw: The reason it was found at all: a ring-shaped basin with 200-300 m rim-to-floor relief, spotted on Google Maps by an amateur. Survives as topography after ~390 Myr.
cfu: ~390 Ma, provisional. Conference abstract only (MetSoc 2026 #5369); no peer-reviewed paper, no stated uncertainty
d1: Spotted on Google Maps by an amateur, confirmed by shatter cones and impact melt in 2025, and named in consultation with the Ekuanitshit Innu. A ring basin 25 km across on Quebec's Cote-Nord that nobody had recognised until someone looked at a satellite image properly.

slw: Buried under Neogene cover.
d1: A confirmed impact structure roughly 25 km across, formed about 50.4 million years ago.

slw: STILL. The best-preserved mid-size crater on Earth; the town of Nordlingen is built inside it and the rim is a visible ring of hills.
ge: Threw moldavite tektites across central Europe — a regional strewn field several hundred km east of the crater — at 14.808 +/- 0.038 Ma.
cfu: 14.808 +/- 0.038 Ma — the single most precisely dated impact structure on Earth
d1: A Miocene crater in Bavaria. Its ejecta scattered glass across central Europe, and the town of Nordlingen is built inside it.

slw: Buried under sediment — which is precisely why its crater-lake record survived intact enough to log a hyperthermal.
ge: Not a cause but a RECORDER, and a valuable one. It struck ~0.65 Myr AFTER the K-Pg extinction, and its crater-lake sediments log the Lower C29n (Dan-C2) hyperthermal in fine detail — a direct archive of how the post-extinction world was recovering, and of a climate excursion that had nothing to do with the impact that made the lake. Pickersgill et al. (2021) raise the possibility that even a 24 km impact could perturb an already-stressed recovery.
cfu: 65.39 +/- 0.14 Ma (Ar-Ar, Pickersgill et al. 2021)
d1: A Ukrainian crater that struck roughly 650,000 years AFTER Chicxulub, into a world still recovering from it. Its lake sediments record that recovery in fine detail.

slw: Structure survives, topography does not. No topographic rim is left after 207 Myr, but the impactites are so well preserved they were quarried as building stone for the local chateaux. Scar life as topography: ~50 Myr.
d1: A confirmed impact structure roughly 23 km across, formed about 206.9 million years ago.

slw: STILL. Lake Lappajarvi fills the crater.
d1: A confirmed impact structure roughly 23 km across, formed about 77.9 million years ago.

slw: STILL. The 5 km central-uplift ring stands 180 m above the desert floor. A textbook orbital image after 142 Myr.
cfu: 142.5 +/- 0.8 Ma (Ar-Ar, Milton & Sutter 1987), corroborated by U-Pb zircon 139 +/- 4 Ma. NOTE: the '165-383 Ma' on Wikipedia's global list is a TARGET-ROCK bracket that leaked into the age column — it is an error
d1: A confirmed impact structure roughly 22 km across, formed about 142.5 million years ago.

slw: STILL. Superbly preserved in polar desert on Devon Island — so well preserved that NASA runs the Haughton-Mars Project and the Flashline Mars station inside it.
cfu: 31.04 +/- 0.37 Ma (Ar-Ar shocked K-feldspar, Erickson et al. 2021)
d1: A confirmed impact structure roughly 23 km across, formed about 31.04 million years ago.

slw: Same burial history as its neighbour Tookoonooka; seismic-only, never drilled.
cfu: ~125 Ma inferred by correlation with Tookoonooka. STRUCTURE ITSELF IS UNCONFIRMED — seismic only, never drilled
d1: A buried structure in Queensland, 84 km across, sitting 300 km from Tookoonooka and apparently the same age. If both are impacts they are the largest known doublet on Earth — but Talundilly has only ever been seen in seismic data, never drilled, so it remains unproven.

slw: Exposed in Saudi desert and confirmed on shocked quartz; the largest confirmed structure on the Arabian Peninsula.
cfu: 70-410 Ma stratigraphic bracket only. A 340 Myr window
d1: The largest confirmed impact structure on the Arabian Peninsula, exposed in the northern Saudi desert and confirmed by shocked quartz. Its age is pinned only between 410 and 70 million years.

slw: STILL, oddly. Concentric ring synclines with salt lakes, strikingly visible from orbit despite an age that may exceed a billion years — Australian cratonic aridity at its most extreme.
cfu: 568-1300 Ma. Ar-Ar K-feldspar older limit ~1300 Ma, K-Ar illite-smectite younger limit ~568 Ma; the authors caution 568 Ma may be a tectonothermal reset. Cannot be placed on either side of 1000 Ma. NO post-2015 redating exists; the '~836 Ma' figure in circulation has no traceable source
d1: Concentric rings of salt lakes in the Western Australian desert, named for Gene Shoemaker, who did more than anyone to establish that craters like this exist. Its age is bracketed only between 1300 and 568 million years — it may not even belong in this timeline.

slw: Buried and confirmed by drilling; the 22 km figure is exterior collapse terrain, not a visible crater.
cfu: ~8 Ma, Late Tortonian. Confirmed only in 2023 on a single paper (Sanchez Gomez et al.); the 22 km is exterior collapse terrain, the true crater is ~5 km
d1: Confirmed only in 2023, and buried: a small Miocene crater in southern Spain whose 22 km footprint is mostly collapsed ground around a true crater a quarter that size.

slw: STILL. A clear annular ridge on the Ennedi Plateau, preserved by Saharan hyperaridity.
cfu: <=383 Ma maximum age only (Devonian-Carboniferous target)
d1: A ring of hills on Chad's Ennedi Plateau. The Sahara's hyperaridity has kept a crater of roughly Devonian age legible as surface topography, which almost nowhere else on Earth manages.

slw: Structurally deformed with no crater morphology left; recognised from shatter cones and strike-slip-style deformation.
cfu: 660-1660 Ma. A 1000 Myr window that straddles the cutoff and cannot be resolved
d1: A crater in the Northern Territory with no crater shape left — it is recognised entirely from shatter cones and sheared rock. Its age could be anywhere in a billion-year window.

slw: Exposed but heavily eroded on the Siberian Traps.
cfu: 40 +/- 20 Ma (50% uncertainty); Impact Earth brackets 23-66 Ma
d1: A Siberian crater punched through the Siberian Traps themselves, so its target rock is the largest flood basalt province on Earth.

slw: Submarine in the Gulf of Finland; the ejecta layer is better known than the crater.
ge: Its ejecta layer, sitting in the pre-trilobite Platysolenites antiquissimus biozone of the Baltic Early Cambrian, is better known and more useful than the crater — it is the sole basis for the ~535 Ma age.
cfu: ~535 Ma, Early Cambrian, BIOSTRATIGRAPHIC only — ejecta sits in the pre-trilobite Platysolenites antiquissimus biozone. No radiometric date. An older ~470 Ma estimate is superseded
d1: A submarine crater in the Gulf of Finland whose ejecta layer is more useful than the crater: it sits in Early Cambrian rocks laid down before trilobites appeared, and is the only reason we know when it struck.

slw: STILL. The central uplift stands out as hills on the West Texas plains, though the crater is deeply eroded.
cfu: <113 Ma (Albian or younger) maximum age only
d1: The central uplift of a West Texas crater, standing as a cluster of hills on otherwise flat plains. Erosion has cut so deep that the crater floor is gone and the plumbing beneath it is exposed.

slw: STILL. Lakes Norra and Sodra Dellen occupy it after 140 Myr.
cfu: 140.82 +/- 0.51 Ma (Ar-Ar). Sharply revised from the legacy 89 Ma
d1: Two lakes in Sweden filling a Cretaceous crater. Long thought to be 89 million years old, it was redated to 141 — one of the larger single-crater corrections in the catalogue.

slw: Eroded in the Little Sandy Desert; defined largely by a ring-shaped aeromagnetic anomaly plus shatter cones.
cfu: <513 Ma maximum age only, from Neoproterozoic-Cambrian cover
d1: A crater in the Little Sandy Desert defined mostly by a ring-shaped magnetic anomaly. Named for Andrew Glikson, who spent a career arguing that Australia was full of unrecognised impact structures.

slw: Buried beneath Dnieper-Donets sediments; no surface expression.
d1: A Jurassic crater buried beneath the Dnieper-Donets basin in Ukraine, with no trace at the surface.

slw: STILL. A near-perfect circular lake in Chukotka, essentially pristine.
ge: No ejecta layer, but a globally important scientific consequence: the ICDP core through its lake sediments yields a continuous 3.6 Myr record of Arctic climate — the longest terrestrial Arctic palaeoclimate archive that exists.
cfu: 3.58 +/- 0.04 Ma (Layer 2000). Independently corroborated by ICDP magnetostratigraphy tuned to 3.580-3.596 Ma. S&K recalculate to 3.65 +/- 0.08 Ma
d1: An almost perfectly circular lake in Chukotka. Because it has never been glaciated, its sediments hold an unbroken 3.6-million-year record of Arctic climate — the longest that exists on land.

slw: Entirely buried in Belarus; found by drilling in the 1970s.
cfu: 29.71 +/- 0.48 Ma (Ar-Ar, Sherlock et al. 2009). The 42.3 +/- 1.1 Ma still on Wikipedia is the superseded pre-2006 EID value
d1: A crater buried under Belarus, found by drilling in the 1970s. Its published age was wrong by 12 million years until Ar-Ar dating moved it to 30 Ma.

slw: Expressed as an 18 km annulus of dolomite hills; the crater form itself is gone but shatter cones, PDFs and impact diamonds remain.
cfu: 476 +/- 8 Ma. Supersedes the stale '>515 Ma' still in circulation
d1: A ring of dolomite hills in Queensland marking a mid-Ordovician impact. The crater is gone; the shatter cones and impact diamonds are not.

slw: Buried ~2.7 km deep in Oklahoma and now a productive oil reservoir in the crater fill.
cfu: 458-478 Ma bracket (Ordovician)
d1: Buried nearly three kilometres deep in Oklahoma, and productive: oil accumulated in the shattered rock of the crater fill, which is how it was found.

slw: STILL. Concentric rings striped by wind-carved yardangs in the Sahara; a classic Landsat and SIR-C image. Hyperaridity has preserved a Devonian crater as surface topography.
cfu: Middle Devonian-Early Mississippian target bracket, ~345-370 Ma. Impact Earth's '0.0035-383 Ma' is effectively no constraint at all
d1: Concentric rings in the Chadian Sahara, combed into stripes by wind-carved yardangs. One of the most photographed craters on Earth from orbit, and possibly one of a chain.

slw: Fully buried in southern Alberta; imaged by seismic and drilling only.
cfu: <65 Ma maximum age only
d1: A crater buried without trace under southern Alberta, mapped only by seismic surveys and drilling.

slw: STILL. An ~11.5 km central ring of hills in the Libyan desert.
cfu: <120 Ma maximum age only
d1: A crater in the Libyan desert whose rim has been stripped down to an inner ring of hills. It sits close to the small BP structure, and the two may be related.

slw: ~15 km apparent structure with a 6 km central uplift; confirmed on PDFs, planar fractures and feather features in quartz rather than on any surviving landform.
cfu: 520-1400 Ma stratigraphic bracket; straddles the cutoff. Confirmed as an impact by Kenkmann et al. 2021 but undated
d1: Confirmed in 2021 on shocked quartz alone, straddling the Northern Territory- Queensland border. Nothing about the landscape suggests a crater; the rock does.

slw: Buried under Devonian-Carboniferous cover; known from boreholes.
cfu: 383-394 Ma bracket (Late Devonian)
d1: A Devonian crater buried under central Russia, known only from boreholes.

slw: STILL. The rim stands 300-350 m above the interior on the Kundelungu Plateau — clearly visible in satellite imagery.
cfu: <=573 Ma maximum age only (post-Neoproterozoic Kundelungu Group)
d1: The first impact structure ever confirmed in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, found in 2011. Its rim rises 300 metres above the interior on the Kundelungu Plateau and is unmistakable from space.

slw: Buried; exposed only inside the Krivoy Rog iron-ore open pits and mine workings.
d1: A Permian crater in Ukraine visible only inside the Krivoy Rog iron-ore pits, where mining has cut through the buried structure.

slw: STILL. A lake-filled basin in Karelia after 687 Myr — the oldest crater on Earth still holding a lake.
d1: A Karelian lake filling a crater 687 million years old — the oldest impact structure on Earth that still holds a lake.

slw: STILL. A young crater basin in the Nicaraguan highlands.
ge: Probable source of the Belize impact glass (0.769 +/- 0.016 Ma). Schmieder & Kring list the source crater as unknown with Pantasma as the candidate, so state this as likely rather than established.
d1: A young crater in the Nicaraguan highlands, and the likely source of the impact glass scattered across Belize 800,000 years ago.

slw: STILL. Excellent exposure and a prominent central uplift ring in near-undeformed Parnaiba Basin sediments.
cfu: <=250 Ma maximum age only (Parnaiba Basin stratigraphy)
d1: Brazil's second-largest crater, cut into flat-lying Parnaiba Basin sandstone. Its central uplift ring is about as clean a textbook example as exists.

slw: STILL, as structure. A well-exposed central uplift with classic shatter cones in Tennessee.
cfu: 100-323 Ma bracket; ~200 Ma is a commonly quoted midpoint with no direct support
d1: A Tennessee crater with a superbly exposed central uplift and shatter cones, long used as a field-teaching site. Its age is bracketed only between 323 and 100 million years.

slw: STILL. A central elevated core rising out of the flat Pampas — highly legible from orbit.
cfu: <=135 Ma maximum age only (post-Serra Geral basalts). No direct date
d1: One of only about three craters on Earth punched into flood basalt. Its central core rises out of the flat Pampas of southern Brazil.

slw: Partially. Exhumed by Quaternary glaciation after being buried; the resurge deposits are exceptionally well preserved.
ge: One of the craters of the mid-Ordovician meteorite shower, the ~470 Ma spike in impact flux following the L-chondrite parent-body breakup. That event is recorded worldwide as fossil meteorites in Swedish and Chinese limestones and is the clearest evidence of a sustained, non-random change in Earth's impact rate. Ames, Clearwater East, Carswell, Tunnunik, Slate Islands and possibly Charlevoix all fall in or near this window — if the app can cluster events, this Ordovician spike is the one worth showing.
cfu: ~455 Ma, tied to Ordovician marine stratigraphy; part of the Ordovician meteorite shower
d1: A Swedish crater formed on a shallow Ordovician sea floor, which is why its resurge deposits — the sediment that washed back in — are the best preserved anywhere. It belongs to the Ordovician meteorite shower that followed the break-up of the L-chondrite parent body.

slw: STILL. A near-perfect circular bay 220 m deep on Reindeer Lake; one of the sharpest crater outlines visible from orbit.
cfu: 95-102 Ma (Albian-Cenomanian palynology)
d1: A circular bay 220 metres deep at the south end of Reindeer Lake, Saskatchewan. Glaciation cleaned it out rather than erasing it, leaving one of the sharpest crater outlines visible from orbit.

slw: STILL. The radiating shatter-cone-bearing sandstone ridges that give it its name are visible from the air after ~740 Myr.
cfu: 580-900 Ma. Younger than the ~900 Ma Yampi Orogeny syncline, older than ~570 Ma cover
d1: Named for the radiating ridges of shatter-coned sandstone that spread from its centre across the Kimberley — the legs are visible from the air after something like 700 million years.

slw: STILL. The youngest structure of its size on Earth; exposed and fresh.
cfu: 0.91 +/- 0.14 Ma (~15%, but on an absolute scale this is very tightly placed)
d1: The youngest crater of its size on Earth, in Kazakhstan, and the source of irghizites — glass droplets thrown from the impact and still lying loose on the surface.

slw: Buried Texas dome; the central uplift is faintly expressed as a topographic high.
d1: A buried Palaeocene dome in Texas, its central uplift showing at the surface as a low rise.

slw: An island-studded lake in the NWT, but heavily glacially scoured — the crater form is largely gone.
d1: A lake full of islands in the Northwest Territories, scoured by ice until little of the crater form was left.

slw: STILL. A 225 m deep depression with a sharp circular rim; three Brazilian municipalities sit inside it.
d1: A crater blasted into the Parana flood basalts, 225 metres deep with a rim so intact that three Brazilian municipalities sit inside it.

slw: Small, buried, minimal expression.
cfu: 4-6 Ma bracket
d1: A small, buried crater on the Russian platform, a few million years old.

slw: Buried under Perth Basin sediments; expressed only as a subtle basin.
cfu: 83.6-89.8 Ma (Coniacian-Santonian stratigraphic bracket). Australia's first confirmed Late Cretaceous impact
d1: Australia's first confirmed Late Cretaceous impact, buried under the Perth Basin and betrayed only by shocked quartz in its breccia.
